newsitem.title: USA: U.S. close to lifting Lebanon travel ban.
newsitem.headline: U.S. close to lifting Lebanon travel ban.

text.p: The United States is on the verge of lifting a 12-year-old ban on U.S. citizens visiting Lebanon, provided Beirut pledges to do more to fight terrorism, a senior State Department official said on Tuesday.
The official said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had not made a final decision but was "inclined to lift the restriction providing there are positive steps by the Lebanese."

Albright was expected to take action in the next 24 hours, said the official, speaking on condition he was not identified. Secretaries of state review the ban every six months, a deadline that falls due on Thursday.

The ban, imposed in 1985 after Moslem zealots hijacked a TWA airliner to Beirut and killed an American passenger, is not watertight, barring American citizens only from using their U.S. passports to visit Lebanon.

It is based on a judgment that Americans face a serious security threat in Lebanon, especially from pro-Iranian Hizbollah guerrillas who remain at large there. The claim is disputed by the Lebanese government.

The U.S. official said steps Lebanon could take to fight terrorism included having its parliament approve the last of 10 covenants on terrorism and hostage-taking, and designating an envoy to discuss anti-terrorism moves with a U.S. team.

The official said that Albright, who is travelling in Asia, had telephoned Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri earlier on Tuesday to ask for increased cooperation and was expected to make further contacts before announcing a decision.

He said that if the ban was lifted, it was expected to be replaced by a strong travel warning telling Americans that Lebanon was still a dangerous place in which the U.S. embassy had only limited scope for helping them.
That would put Lebanon in a category with such countries as Sudan, Afghanistan, Algeria, Colombia and Iran, instead of bracketing it with Iraq and Libya, to which travel is banned.
Easing the restriction would "send a powerful signal that we want to see Lebanon become an independent, thriving nation," the U.S. official said.

The travel ban has been widely ignored, especially by some 40,000 Lebanese-American dual nationals who visit Beirut each year, but Lebanese officials say it continues to put a damper on business relations between the two countries.

Since Lebanon's civil war ended in 1991, U.S. leaders have several times been tempted to end the ban in order to increase Lebanon's independence from its patron Syria and boost the standing of Hariri, who is well-liked in Washington.

But the administration has remained haunted by memories of the 1980s, when 241 U.S. servicemen died in a 1983 suicide truck bombing at a Marine base in Beirut and dozens of other Americans died in two bomb attacks on embassy buildings.
Still other Americans were held hostage in Lebanon for years in the late 1980s by Iranian-backed guerrillas.

Lebanese officials contend that their country is now safer than many that Americans are not banned from visiting. They have portrayed the ban as U.S. pressure on Lebanon to join peace talks with Israel.
